nameStory: Donn's Grimmia honors James Donn, an 18th-century British botanist who served as curator of the Cambridge Botanic Garden. Like many mosses named after early botanists, this tiny plant carries the legacy of someone who spent countless hours peering through hand lenses at these miniature marvels. The name 'Grimmia' itself comes from Johann Friedrich Carl Grimm, a German physician and bryologist who studied these rock-loving mosses.
description: Donn's Grimmia is a tiny cushion moss that forms dense, dark green to blackish patches on rocks and stone surfaces. Each individual plant is barely noticeable, but together they create velvety cushions that rarely exceed an inch across. This is one of the smaller members of the rock moss family, creating compact mounds that hug tightly to their rocky homes. When dry, the cushions turn almost black and feel crispy, but a few drops of water quickly revive them to a rich green.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms very small, dense cushions that feel like tiny velvet pillows pressed against rock surfaces, rarely more than half an inch tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely small, narrow leaves that overlap like tiny scales and curl inward when dry, requiring a hand lens to see individual leaf details

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dramatically changes from rich green when wet to dark brown or nearly black when dry, making it almost invisible on dark rocks

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on hard rock surfaces, especially granite or other acidic rocks, never on soil or tree bark

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels crispy and brittle when dry, like touching dried herbs, but becomes soft and spongy within seconds of getting wet

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: [UNCERTAIN] Small, dark capsules on short stalks may appear in spring, though sporophytes are rarely seen in this species

habitat: Look for Donn's Grimmia on exposed rock faces, particularly granite outcrops and acidic stone surfaces in mountainous areas of New England. It prefers spots that get some moisture but also experience periods of complete drying, such as rock ledges that catch morning dew or occasional rainfall. This moss is most commonly found at higher elevations where temperature fluctuations and exposure create the harsh conditions it thrives in.

seasonality.spring: Cushions begin to green up with increased moisture, and any sporophytes would be most visible now, though they're rarely produced. Spring rains make identification easier as the moss shows its true green color.
seasonality.summer: Often appears completely dead during dry spells, turning dark brown to black and becoming nearly invisible against dark rock. Best found early in the morning when dew reveals the cushions.
seasonality.fall: Autumn rains revive the cushions, making this a good time for identification as the moss alternates between wet-green and dry-dark phases. Color changes are most dramatic in fall weather.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often hidden under snow or ice, though mild winter days may reveal active green cushions on sun-warmed rock faces.

funFact: Donn's Grimmia can survive being completely dried out for months, losing up to 95% of its water content and appearing completely dead, then spring back to vibrant life within 30 seconds of getting wet—faster than you can say the moss's full scientific name!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small Grimmia species, especially Grey-cushioned Grimmia, but Donn's Grimmia forms much smaller, tighter cushions that turn darker when dry. Memory trick: 'Donn's is Done small'—it makes the tiniest cushions of the common rock mosses.
contextualKnowledge: [UNCERTAIN] With only one recorded observation in New England, Donn's Grimmia may be extremely rare in our region or possibly misidentified in collections. Moss identification often requires expert verification, and this species might be more common than records suggest due to its tiny size and seasonal invisibility.
compareHints: Compared to Grey-cushioned Grimmia, Donn's Grimmia forms much smaller, more compact cushions and turns darker when dry. Unlike Dry Rock Moss (Grimmia pilifera), it lacks the distinctive hair-pointed leaves that give that species a greyish appearance. [UNCERTAIN] Donn's Grimmia is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and very dense growth form among the New England Grimmia species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Grimmia Dry Rock Moss differs from Grey-cushioned Grimmia by having more pronounced white hair-tips and forming tighter, more dome-like cushions rather than looser mats.
Unlike Grimmia Dry Rock Moss which tends to form flatter mats, grey-cushioned grimmia creates more pronounced, dome-shaped cushions.
